rewrites.summary:
Taraba stands under Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act criminalises arranging, attending or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation anywhere in the country, and notes that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice. The same reporting era records mass arrests and detentions of LGBTQ+ people as common, especially in northern states, and the August 2024 beating death of a widely followed transgender content creator in the federal capital — hours after a public post, with the murder left unsolved — evidences lethal violence against visibly trans people.

The source material does not place Taraba among the states/provinces that add religious (Sharia) criminal provisions reaching death-penalty outcomes, and no Taraba-specific finding is documented in either direction. The visitor's profile here is therefore the national one: criminalisation on the statute book, arbitrary enforcement, and little protection against mob or individual violence.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Neighbour comparison: framework sources report that some northern states/provinces applying religious (Sharia) criminal provisions can prescribe the death penalty for same-sex conduct, with penalties ranging from lashing or caning up to death; the sources do not name Taraba among that group.

National enforcement context: a 2016 human-rights report records that passage of the prohibition act in January 2014 was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering; the report is national in scope and names no Taraba-specific case. No litigation flux in the parent nation is documented in this record's sources.

This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score, and no sub-national divergence for a visitor is documented in the sources: no enacted bylaw, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people and no protective legislation for this province.

A visitor stands under the national framework the sources document: the parent nation provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, and the national penal code in force from 2 January 2026 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The province's own reference page documents an overwhelmingly conservative religious character and a tourism-dependent economy, which condition the social environment any visitor moves through; the moral-restriction provisions of the national code operate in that setting, and visible trans or queer presence will meet cultural hostility in everyday settings.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National policy turbulence: the penal code was passed by the national parliament in December 2022, with the outside-marriage restriction set to take effect on 2 January 2026. An August 2026 feature on growing repression of the country's transgender community was navigation-only at fetch, so its content stands only on its headline and the dossier summary.

Comparisons with neighbours: the framework source records that in one province homosexuality is illegal under religious law with flogging or imprisonment, and that police raids on gay gatherings continue elsewhere — 75 people arrested at a private gathering near the capital on 22 June 2025, plus raids in the capital region in February and May 2025 — none of it documented for this province.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data: the province is overwhelmingly Muslim — 96.88% of residents per 2022 government data, with an estimated mid-2025 population of about 5.7 million — with a conservative religious character and a tourism-dependent economy, and the majority local ethnic group of the larger island preserves strong traditions, including a form of Islam influenced by local beliefs and documented as the official religion of the region's historical rulers. A national survey of residents cited for 2025 found a large majority labelling homosexuality morally unacceptable, and conversion therapy is widely practiced in the country.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The province's own reference page contains no LGBT-specific statute or incident, and no sub-national divergence is documented in either direction; absence of evidence is not proof of local practice. The August 2026 feature on growing repression was navigation-only at fetch, so its claims rest on the headline and the dossier summary. The 2025 survey figure and the 2022 government demographic data are the only attributed numbers in the record, and the penal-code provisions took effect only in January 2026, so enforcement practice is not yet observable from the dossier. No source in the dossier addresses border-screening, documents or passport-marker practice for trans visitors.

The audited sources for this province are national-level and were only partly retrievable: a 2022 wire report on police denying mistreatment after a foreign transgender activist died on drug charges while in custody in another province (named as Bali in the source's account; page unretrievable at fetch, available only as a fetch-time summary), and an August 2026 feature on growing repression of the country's transgender community, navigation-only at fetch, standing on its headline and the dossier summary.

No province-specific statute, ordinance, raid, protection or service is documented in anything examined, so a visitor stands under the national picture those sources sketch: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, rising official and vigilante hostility toward LGBT+ visibility, and weak accountability for mob violence. One national-framework detail bears directly on documents: since June 2021 the national home-affairs ministry has run outreach issuing identity papers to transgender people, and this province is among the nine whose transgender residents have benefited so far — evidence that identity-document issuance for transgender people has operated here since mid-2021, which bears on document status and enrolment for trans travellers to this division.

The national position a visitor stands under, per the framework sources: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no anti-discrimination protections, no X-marker, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage. The national penal code, in force from 2 January 2026, criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member — and because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction; the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships. Document status: since June 2021 the national home-affairs ministry has run outreach issuing identity papers to transgender residents, with only male and female sex descriptors recognised and birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained, and electronic identity cards issued in nine provinces.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National policy turbulence: the penal code was passed by the national parliament on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment; international criticism has faulted the code for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and domestic partnerships. An August 2026 feature on growing repression of the country's transgender community was navigation-only at fetch, standing on headline and dossier summary.

Comparisons with neighbours: the framework source records raids on transgender women by the social agency of the capital and the January 2021 flogging of two men under religious law in one province — enforcement textures reported outside this province.
